summary: Presents an architecture for differentiated services on the Internet that uses two bits in the packet header, enough to offer a premium and an assured service. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes a way to give some internet traffic a better service than the rest, using two bits in the packet header. One bit marks traffic that has been promised a fixed top speed, and another marks traffic that should be dropped later than ordinary traffic when a queue fills. The memo also explains how neighbouring networks agree on how much of each they will carry for one another.

subtitle: Two bits in the IP header, two kinds of service, and a way for neighbouring networks to agree on how much of each to carry.

tldr.problem: The Internet offers one service to everything: best effort. Two separate proposals had worked out how to give one class of traffic a better service using a single bit of the IP header, but they were different services with different policies and neither had been standardised.
tldr.mechanism: The memo puts the two proposals in one architecture, marking packets with a Premium bit or an Assured bit taken from the IP header precedence field. Premium packets get their own high-priority queue; Assured packets are dropped later than ordinary ones. Allocation of the two services is handled by bandwidth brokers in each domain, which negotiate with the broker next door.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and describes a reference architecture rather than a standard. It was published as a record of the thinking that fed into RFCs 2474 and 2475, and it recommends incremental deployment with conservative amounts of marked traffic.

facts.label: Premium queue size at a router
facts.value: on the order of ten packets

today: RFC 2638 is an Informational memo from July 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It was originally submitted as an Internet draft in November 1997, and the memo says it is published in its original form as a record of where the thinking was at that time, not as an indication of future direction. Its ideas, together with Dave Clark's December 1997 presentation, were key to the work that led to RFCs 2474 and 2475.

sections.title: What the Architecture Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
Dave Clark and Van Jacobson each presented work at the Munich IETF meeting on how to use one bit of the IP header to deliver a new kind of service to packets. The two presentations were very different kinds of service with quite different policy assumptions, and the discussion that followed convinced the authors that both have merit and that both can be implemented with a set of very similar mechanisms.

The memo proposes an architectural framework that permits the use of both service types and exploits their similarities in the forwarding path. The major goals are shared with one or both of the original proposals: keep the forwarding path simple, push complexity to the edges of the network to the extent possible, provide a service that avoids assumptions about the type of traffic using it, employ an allocation policy that will be compatible with both long-term and short-term provisioning, and make it possible for the dominant Internet traffic model to remain best-effort.

The memo says it contributes two distinct service types, a set of general mechanisms for the forwarding path that can implement a range of differentiated services, and a flexible framework for provisioning a differentiated services network. The argument is that this is the kind of architecture needed for expedient deployment: a framework and set of primitives that can be implemented in the short term and provide interoperable services, yet can also provide a sandbox for experimentation that can lead in time to more levels of differentiation within each service.

The authors include an analogy with airline classes of service, and stress one part of it: best-effort traffic, like coach class seats on an airplane, is still expected to make up the bulk of Internet traffic, while business and first class carry a small number of passengers but matter to the economics of the industry. They do not expect differentiated services to comprise all Internet traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people had each designed a way to give one class of traffic a better service using a single bit in the packet header. The authors argue that the two designs are compatible and can share the same equipment, so a network can offer both. The design keeps the routers in the middle of the network simple and pushes the complicated decisions to the edges, where there are fewer flows to keep track of.

sections.title: Two Services From One Bit Each
sections.content:
The current Internet delivers one type of service, best-effort, to all traffic. The memo focuses on two particular ways of adding a differentiated level of service, each designated by one bit. Both seek to define a single common mechanism used by interior network routers, pushing most of the complexity and state of differentiated services to the network edges, and both use bandwidth as the resource being requested and allocated.

Clark and Wroclawski defined an Assured service that follows expected capacity usage profiles and is statistically provisioned. The assurance a user gets is that such traffic is unlikely to be dropped as long as it stays within the expected capacity profile; the exact meaning of unlikely depends on how well the service is provisioned. An Assured flow may exceed its profile, but the excess traffic is not given the same assurance level. This service uses buffer management to provide a better-effort service.

Jacobson defined a Premium service provisioned according to peak capacity profiles that are strictly not oversubscribed, and that is given its own high-priority queue in routers. A Premium flow is shaped and hard-limited to its provisioned peak rate, and shaped so that bursts are not injected into the network. Premium presents a virtual wire: a flow's bursts may queue at the shaper at the edge of the network, but thereafter only in proportion to the indegree of each router. This creates a service with little jitter and queueing delay and no need for queue management on the Premium queue.

Despite the similarities, the two approaches result in fundamentally different services. Premium allocates a small percentage of total network capacity but prices it much higher; one use is to create virtual leased lines, saving the cost of building and maintaining a separate network. Whenever the allocated capacity is not being used it is available to best-effort traffic. Assured permits flows to use any additional available capacity without penalty, and occasional dropped packets during short congestive periods may be acceptable to many users, which is what an ISP might offer to individual customers willing to pay a little more for a service that seems unaffected by congestion. Both services are only as good as their admission control schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: The two services differ in what they promise. Premium promises a fixed top speed, never shares its bandwidth, and is given priority in every router, so it queues very little. Assured promises only that traffic inside the agreed profile is unlikely to be dropped, and can borrow spare capacity when there is some. Premium suits applications that need a steady rate, such as a voice call; Assured suits traffic that must not be lost but can wait.

sections.title: The Forwarding Path: Markers and Profile Meters
sections.content:
The forwarding path mechanisms divide into those that happen at the input interface, before packet forwarding, and those that happen at the output interface, after it. Intermediate routers only need the post-forwarding functions, while leaf and border routers must also act on arriving packets before forwarding.

Leaf routers are configured with a traffic profile for a particular flow, based on its packet header. All arriving packets must have both the A-bit and the P-bit cleared, after which packets are classified on their header. A packet whose header matches no configured value is immediately forwarded. Matched flows pass through individual Markers configured from the usage profile for that flow: service class, rate, and permissible burst size. Assured flow packets emerge from the Marker with their A-bits set when the flow is in conformance to its profile. For a Premium flow, the Marker holds packets when necessary to enforce the configured rate, so Premium flow packets emerge shaped with their P-bits set.

Inside the Marker is a token bucket that fills at the flow rate from the usage profile. For Assured service the bucket depth is set by the profile's burst size; for Premium the bucket depth must be limited to the equivalent of only one or two packets, with a depth of one packet suggested in early deployments. When a token is present, Assured flow packets have their A-bit set; otherwise the packet is passed on unchanged. For a Premium-configured Marker, arriving packets that see a token are marked and forwarded, and when no token is present the packets are held until one arrives. If a Premium flow bursts enough to overflow the holding queue, its packets are dropped. The bucket is implemented in bytes, and a token counts as present if the number of bytes in the bucket is equal to or larger than the size of the packet. For Premium the bucket can only fill to the maximum packet size, while Assured may fill to the configured burst parameter.

Each output interface of a router must have two queues and must implement a test on the P-bit to select a packet's output queue, with the two queues serviced by simple priority, Premium packets first. Each output interface must implement the RED-based RIO mechanism on the lower priority queue. RIO uses two thresholds for when to begin dropping packets: a lower one based on total queue occupancy for ordinary best-effort traffic, and one based on the number of packets enqueued that have their A-bit set. Any action preferential to Assured traffic is therefore taken only when the queue's capacity exceeds the threshold for ordinary traffic, and only unmarked packets are dropped using the RED algorithm unless the Assured threshold is also reached.

At the boundary between two domains there is a Profile Meter. A Profile Meter is required at the ingress of a trust region to ensure that differentiated service flows comply with their agreed rates. Non-compliant Premium packets are discarded, while non-compliant Assured packets have their A-bits reset. The simplest form is a token bucket configured with the contracted rate across that ingress link, and each service type on each interface needs its own profile meter.
sections.plainLanguage: At the edge of the network a router looks at the packet header, matches it against the flows it has been configured for, and marks it. The marking uses a token bucket that fills at the agreed rate: for a Premium flow the packet waits for a token, which holds the traffic back to exactly the promised speed; for an Assured flow the token is simply a yes or no, and the packet is marked only if one is available. In the middle of the network, routers do very little: they look at the Premium bit to pick one of two queues, and serve the Premium queue first. At a border, a Profile Meter checks the incoming marked traffic against the rate agreed with the neighbouring network.

sections.title: Bandwidth Brokers and Allocation
sections.content:
Most organisations have fixed portions of their budgets determined annually or quarterly, and service providers plan on the same cycle, so they cannot be expected to provide differentiated services purely on call. Provisioning sets up static levels of marked traffic, while call set-up creates an allocation for a single flow's duration. The memo uses Allocation for the whole process, and requires an architecture that can encompass the entire spectrum from strictly preallocated to dynamic call set-up, in any mix. Allocation must follow organisational hierarchies, and the only chance of success for incremental deployment lies in an architecture made up of bilateral agreements, since multilateral agreements are much too complex to administer.

The control of the sharing can be done independently by individuals, who set bits in their own packets, but the memo argues that is simple to implement yet unlikely to be sufficient, since it is unreasonable to expect all individuals to know their organisation's priorities and current network use. The architecture therefore uses agents called bandwidth brokers, which can be configured with organisational policies, keep track of the current allocation of marked traffic, and interpret new requests to mark traffic in the light of those policies and the current allocation. Brokers need only a relationship of limited trust with their peers in adjacent domains, unlike schemes that require flow specifications to be set in every router along an end-to-end path. Organisationaly, the broker architecture lets end-to-end services be built out of purely bilateral agreements, and it keeps state on an administrative domain basis rather than at every router, while the service definitions confine per-flow state to just the leaf routers.

A broker has two responsibilities. Its primary one is to parcel out its region's marked traffic allocations and set up the leaf routers within the local domain. The other is to manage the messages sent across boundaries to adjacent regions' brokers. A broker has a policy database recording who can do what and when, and a method of using that database to authenticate requesters. Only a broker can configure the leaf routers to deliver a particular service to flows, which is crucial for deploying a secure system. Each domain's broker establishes a secure association with its peer in the adjacent domain to negotiate or configure a rate and a service class across the shared boundary; in early implementations this may be accomplished by human negotiation and subsequent manual configuration rather than automatically.

When an allocation is desired, a request is sent to the broker. Requests include a service type, a target rate, a maximum burst and the time period when service is required, and may be made by a network administrator, a user or another region's broker. The broker first authenticates the requester, then verifies that unallocated bandwidth sufficient to meet the request exists. If the request passes, the available bandwidth is reduced by the requested amount and the flow specification is recorded. Where the flow has a destination outside the trust region, the request must fall within the class allocation established through the bilateral agreement with the next-hop region, and the requester's broker informs the adjacent region's broker that it will be using some of that rate. The broker configures the leaf router with the information about the packet flow, and that configuration is soft state that the broker periodically refreshes. The adjacent broker is responsible for configuring its border router to permit the allocated flow to pass. All agreements and negotiations are between two adjacent domains, so an initial request might cause communication between brokers on several domains along a path, but each communication is only between two adjacent brokers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each organisation has an agent, the bandwidth broker, that keeps a record of how much of its marked traffic has been promised and to whom. A request arrives with a service, a rate and a time. The broker checks who is allowed to ask, checks that there is enough unpromised capacity, records the promise, and tells the edge routers which packets to mark. If the destination is in another organisation's network, the broker tells that organisation's broker, and so on down the path, one neighbour at a time.

sections.title: Working With RSVP and Integrated Services
sections.content:
The memo argues that the forwarding path mechanisms described in its third section are general enough to provide the Controlled-Load service and a version of the Guaranteed Quality of Service, as developed by the Integrated Services working group. Premium service can be thought of as a constrained case of Controlled-Load service where the burst size is limited to one packet and where non-conforming packets are dropped, so a router that implements Premium can support the more general Controlled-Load service by lifting the constraint on the token bucket size, or by configuring the Premium rate with the peak traffic rate parameter of the Controlled-Load specification, and by changing the policing action on out-of-profile packets from dropping to sending them to the best-effort queue.

It is also possible to implement Guaranteed service using the Premium mechanisms, because the service model of Premium clearly fits that model, and because RFC 2212 states that non-conforming datagrams should be treated as best-effort datagrams. A policing Profile Meter that drops non-conforming datagrams would therefore be acceptable, though the action could also be changed from a drop to sending the packet to the best-effort queue.

The memo then considers how RSVP signalling could work with the brokers. It lists three differences from the original RSVP resource set-up model. There exist prior bilateral business relations between brokers of adjacent trust regions before end-to-end resource allocation can be set up, and real-time signalling is used only to activate or confirm the availability of pre-negotiated marked bandwidth and to readjust the allocation amount when necessary. A few bits in the packet header, the P-bit and A-bit, mark the service class of each packet, so a full packet classification by checking all relevant header fields need be done only once at the leaf router. And RSVP resource set-up assumes that resources are reserved hop by hop at each router along the entire end-to-end path, which the broker architecture does not require.

RSVP messages sent to leaf routers by hosts can be intercepted and sent to the local domain's broker instead. The broker processes the message and, if the request is approved, forwards a message to the leaf router that sets up the appropriate per-flow packet classification, and a message should also be sent to the egress border router to add to the aggregate marked traffic allocation for shaping by the Profile Meter on outbound traffic. An RSVP message must be sent across the boundary to the adjacent ISP's border router, and inside a domain packets are served solely according to the marked bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The same router mechanisms can also deliver the older Integrated Services, such as Controlled-Load and Guaranteed, with a few parameter changes. The memo also shows how the signalling protocol RSVP could be used with the broker arrangement: instead of a message travelling hop by hop through every router, it goes to the local broker, which approves it and then tells the edge routers what to do. That saves the state and the work that hop-by-hop reservation would need.

sections.title: Deployment Recommendations and Security
sections.content:
The memo presents a reference architecture and says several variations can be envisioned, particularly for early and partial deployments. Its conclusion is that it is both possible and feasible to start deployment of differentiated services incrementally: given that the basic mechanisms required in the packet forwarding path are clearly understood, both Assured and Premium services can be implemented today with manually configured brokers and static resource allocation, and the recommendation is to make conservative choices about the amount of marked traffic admitted into the network.

The authors plan to continue the effort started with the memo and their experimental work to define and deploy increasingly sophisticated brokers, hoping to turn the experience gained from trial implementations on ESNet and CAIRN into future proposals to the IETF. Future revisions of the memo are to present receiver-based and multicast flow allocations in detail. The main intent is to define an architecture with three services, Premium, Assured and Best Effort, determined by specific bit patterns, but not to preclude additional levels of differentiation within each service. The base-level approach is that everyone has to provide at least Premium service and Assured service as documented, and the architecture has to be open-ended so that more levels of differentiation might be standardised in future.

The security section is one line: there are no security considerations associated with this document. The security requirements that the text does raise are administrative rather than protocol ones. Only a broker can configure the leaf routers to deliver a particular service to flows, which the memo calls crucial for deploying a secure system, and the configuration information that reaches a leaf router has to be authenticated in some way, with the method left for future standards work.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is to start small: set the two mechanisms up, use manually configured brokers, and admit only a small amount of marked traffic at first. The memo's security section says there is nothing to report, but it does rely on two rules elsewhere: only the broker may tell the edge routers what to do, and whatever tells the broker to do so has to be authenticated.

cells: Peak capacity profiles, strictly not oversubscribed
Traffic is unlikely to be dropped while inside the profile
The same as undropped best-effort packets
The flow is hard-limited to the peak rate
The excess traffic is not given the same assurance
Dropped later than unmarked packets in the normal queue
None; the allocation is never oversubscribed
May use any additional capacity without penalty

viz.caption: THE SIX FORWARDING PATH PRIMITIVES (RFC 2638 SECTION 3.1)

items.title: General classifier
items.text: Matches a flow on the packet header tuple, at the edge of the network.

items.title: Bit-pattern classifier
items.text: Reads the P-bit and A-bit to pick a queue and a drop policy.

items.title: Bit setter
items.text: Sets or clears the service bits in the IP header.

items.title: Priority queues
items.text: Two levels, with the Premium queue served first.

items.title: Shaping token bucket
items.text: Holds packets back so a Premium flow leaves at exactly its rate.

items.title: Policing token bucket
items.text: Never holds packets; drops or unmarks those over the agreed rate.
